7He stretches out the northern sky over empty space;
he hangs the earth on nothing.
8He wraps up the waters in his clouds,
yet the clouds do not burst under their weight.
9He veils the face of his throne,
spreading his cloud over it.
10He has marked out a circle on the face of the waters
as a boundary between light and darkness.
11The pillars of heaven tremble
and are stunned at his rebuke.
12By his power he stirred up the sea;
by his skill he struck Rahab down.
13By his breath the skies became clear;
his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
14Look, these are only the outer edges of his ways;
how faint the whisper we hear of him!
But the thunder of his power, who can understand it?
fields.summary: Job describes God’s power over the depths and the heavens, which are only the edges of God’s ways.

fields.title: Job 27
fields.body_html:
Job holds fast to his integrity

1Job took up his discourse again and said:
2As God lives, who has denied me justice,
and the Almighty, who has made my life bitter,
3as long as I still have breath in me
and the breath of God is in my nostrils,
4my lips will not speak what is wrong,
and my tongue will not utter lies.
5Far be it from me to say that you are right;
until I die
I will not give up my integrity.
6I hold on to my righteousness and will not let it go;
my conscience does not blame me
for any day of my life.
7Let my enemy be like the wicked,
and my opponent like the unrighteous.
8For what hope does the godless have when God cuts him off,
when he takes away his life?
9Will God hear his cry
when trouble comes upon him?
10Will he find delight in the Almighty?
Will he call on God at all times?
11I will teach you about the power of God;
what the Almighty has in mind
I will not hide.
12Look, all of you have seen it for yourselves;
why then do you talk such empty nonsense?
13This is the portion a wicked person has from God,
the inheritance the ruthless receive from the Almighty:
14If his children are many, they are destined for the sword,
and his descendants will never have enough to eat.
15Those who survive him will be buried by the plague,
and his widows will not mourn.
16Though he piles up silver like dust
and stores up clothes like heaps of clay,
17he may store them up, but the righteous will wear them,
and the innocent will divide up the silver.
18The house he builds is like a moth’s cocoon,
like a shelter put up by a watchman.
19He lies down rich, but he will not be gathered to his ancestors;
he opens his eyes, and he is gone.
20Terrors overtake him like a flood;
in the night a storm carries him off.
21The east wind picks him up, and he is gone;
it sweeps him away from his place.
22It hurls itself at him without mercy,
as he flees headlong from its power.
23It claps its hands at him
and hisses at him from his place.
fields.summary: Job holds fast to his integrity and describes the fate of the wicked.

fields.title: Job 28
fields.body_html:
There is a mine for silver

1There is a mine for silver
and a place where gold is refined.
2Iron is taken from the earth,
and copper is smelted from ore.
3Miners put an end to darkness;
they search to the farthest limits
for ore in gloom and deep darkness.
4They cut a shaft far from where people live,
in places forgotten by those who walk above;
they hang and swing far from other people.
5From the earth comes bread,
but underneath it is turned upside down as if by fire.
6Its rocks are where sapphires are found,
and its dust contains gold.
7No bird of prey knows that path;
the falcon’s eye has never seen it.
8Proud beasts have not set foot on it;
the lion has never passed along it.
9Miners put their hand to the flinty rock
and overturn mountains at their roots.
10They cut tunnels through the rocks,
and their eyes see every treasure.
11They dam up the trickling streams,
and bring hidden things out into the light.

But where can wisdom be found?

12But where can wisdom be found?
Where is the place of understanding?
13No human being knows its worth;
it is not found in the land of the living.
14The deep says, “It is not in me,”
and the sea says, “It is not with me.”
15It cannot be bought with the finest gold,
and its price cannot be weighed out in silver.
16It cannot be weighed against the gold of Ophir,
against precious onyx or sapphire.
17Gold and glass cannot equal it,
nor can it be traded for articles of fine gold.
18Coral and crystal are not worth mentioning;
the price of wisdom is beyond rubies.
19The topaz of Cush cannot equal it;
it cannot be weighed against pure gold.

God understands the way to wisdom

20Then where does wisdom come from?
Where is the place of understanding?
21It is hidden from the eyes of every living creature,
concealed even from the birds of the sky.
22Abaddon and Death say,
“We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.”
23God understands the way to it,
and he alone knows its place.
24For he looks to the ends of the earth
and sees everything under the heavens.
25When he gave the wind its weight
and measured out the waters,
26when he made a law for the rain
and a path for the thunder and lightning,
27then he saw wisdom and appraised it;
he set it in place and searched it through.
28And he said to humankind,
“Look, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom,
and to turn away from evil is understanding.”
fields.summary: Silver and gold come from the earth, but wisdom cannot be found or bought. God alone knows its place: the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

fields.title: Job 29
fields.body_html:
Job remembers the days when God watched over him

1Then Job took up his discourse again:
2Oh, that I were as in the months gone by,
as in the days when God watched over me,
3when his lamp shone above my head,
and by his light I walked through the darkness,
4as I was in the days of my prime,
when God’s friendship was over my tent,
5when the Almighty was still with me
and my children were all around me,
6when my steps were bathed in cream,
and the rock poured out streams of olive oil for me!
7When I went out to the city gate
and took my seat in the public square,
8the young men saw me and stepped aside,
and the old men rose and stood;
9officials stopped talking
and put their hands over their mouths;
10the voices of the nobles fell silent,
and their tongues stuck to the roofs of their mouths.
11When anyone heard me, they called me blessed,
and when anyone saw me, they spoke well of me,
12because I rescued the poor who cried for help
and the fatherless who had no one to help them.
13The blessing of those who were about to perish came upon me,
and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy.
14I put on righteousness, and it clothed me;
my justice was like a robe and a turban.
15I was eyes for the blind
and feet for the lame.
16I was a father to the needy,
and I looked into the case of the stranger.
17I broke the fangs of the wicked
and made them drop their prey from their teeth.
18I said, I will die in my own nest,
and my days will be as many as the grains of sand.
19My roots reach out to the water,
and the dew lies all night on my branches.
20My honor stays fresh with me,
and my bow is ever new in my hand.
21People listened to me and waited;
they kept silent for my advice.
22After I spoke, they did not speak again;
my words fell on them like drops of rain.
23They waited for me as for the rain
and opened their mouths wide as for the spring rain.
24I smiled on them when they had lost confidence,
and they did not cast down the light of my face.
25I chose the way for them and sat as their chief;
I lived like a king among his troops, like one who comforts those who mourn.
fields.summary: Job remembers his former days, when he was honored at the city gate and helped the poor and the fatherless.

fields.title: Job 30
fields.body_html:
But now they laugh at me

1But now they laugh at me,
men younger than I am,
whose fathers I would have refused
to put with my sheepdogs.
2What use to me was the strength of their hands,
men whose vigor was gone?
3Gaunt with want and hunger,
they gnawed the dry ground,
in the gloom of waste and desolation.
4They pick salt plants among the bushes,
and the roots of the broom tree are their food.
5They are driven out from human company;
people shout after them as after a thief.
6They have to live on the slopes of the dry ravines,
in holes in the ground and among the rocks.
7They bray among the bushes
and huddle together under the nettles.
8A senseless and nameless brood,
they were driven out of the land with whips.
9And now I have become their mocking song;
I have become a byword among them.
10They detest me and keep their distance from me;
they do not hesitate to spit in my face.
11Because God has loosened my bowstring and humbled me,
they have thrown off all restraint in my presence.
12On my right the rabble rises up;
they trip up my feet
and build their siege ramps of ruin against me.
13They break up my path;
they help my destruction along,
and no one holds them back.
14They come in as through a wide breach in the wall;
amid the crash of ruins they roll on.
15Terrors are turned against me;
my honor is driven away as by the wind,
and my safety has vanished like a cloud.
16And now my life is poured out within me;
days of suffering have taken hold of me.
17At night my bones are pierced within me,
and the pains that gnaw at me never rest.
18With great force my clothing is twisted out of shape;
it binds me like the collar of my tunic.
19He has thrown me into the mud,
and I have become like dust and ashes.
20I cry to you for help, but you do not answer me;
I stand up, and you merely look at me.
21You have turned cruel toward me;
with the strength of your hand you attack me.
22You lift me up on the wind and make me ride it;
you toss me about in the roar of the storm.
23For I know that you will bring me to death,
to the house appointed for all the living.
24Yet does not someone in ruins stretch out a hand,
and cry for help in his disaster?
25Did I not weep for those in trouble?
Did I not grieve for the needy?
26Yet when I hoped for good, evil came;
when I waited for light, darkness came.
27My insides churn and are never still;
days of suffering confront me.
28I go about blackened, but not by the sun;
I stand up in the assembly and cry for help.
29I have become a brother to jackals
and a companion to ostriches.
30My skin turns black and peels from me,
and my bones burn with fever.
31My lyre is tuned to mourning,
and my flute to the sound of weeping.
fields.summary: Now young men mock Job, and he cries to God without answer, his skin blackened and his harp turned to mourning.

fields.title: Job 31
fields.body_html:
A covenant with my eyes

1I made a covenant with my eyes;
how then could I look with desire at a young woman?
2For what portion does God above assign,
what inheritance does the Almighty give from on high?
3Is it not ruin for the unrighteous,
and disaster for those who do evil?
4Does he not see my ways
and count every step I take?
5If I have walked with falsehood,
or my foot has hurried after deceit,
6let him weigh me on honest scales,
and let God know my integrity.
7If my steps have turned from the path,
if my heart has followed my eyes,
or if any stain has clung to my hands,
8then let me sow and another eat,
and let my crops be uprooted.
9If my heart has been lured by a woman,
or I have lurked at my neighbor’s door,
10then let my wife grind grain for another man,
and let other men lie with her.
11For that would be a shameful crime,
a wrong to be punished by the judges.
12It is a fire that burns all the way to Abaddon,
and it would root out all my harvest.
13If I have refused justice to my male or female servants
when they brought a complaint against me,
14what would I do when God rises up?
When he calls me to account, what answer would I give him?
15Did not the one who made me in the womb make them too?
Did not the same God form us both in the womb?
16If I have refused the poor what they longed for,
or let the widow’s eyes grow weary with waiting,
17or eaten my bread alone,
and not shared it with the orphan,
18for from my youth the orphan grew up with me as with a father,
and from my mother’s womb I have guided the widow;
19if I have seen anyone dying for lack of clothing,
or the needy with nothing to cover them,
20if their bodies have not blessed me
because they were warmed with the fleece of my sheep,
21if I have raised my hand against the orphan
because I saw I had support at the city gate,
22then let my shoulder fall from its blade,
and let my arm be broken off at the socket.
23For I dreaded disaster from God,
and because of his majesty I could not do such things.
24If I have put my confidence in gold,
or said to fine gold, “You are my security,”
25if I have rejoiced because my wealth was great,
because my hand had gained so much,
26if I have looked at the sun when it shone,
or the moon moving in its splendor,
27and my heart has been secretly enticed,
so that I threw them a kiss with my hand,
28this too would be a crime to be punished by the judges,
for I would have been false to God above.
29If I have rejoiced at the ruin of someone who hated me,
or gloated when disaster overtook them,
30I have not let my mouth sin
by calling down a curse on their life.
31If the people of my household have not said,
“Who has not had their fill of his meat?”
32No outsider had to spend the night in the street,
for I opened my doors to the traveler.
33If I have concealed my transgressions as people do,
by hiding my guilt in my heart,
34because I feared the great crowd
and the contempt of the clans terrified me,
so that I kept quiet and would not go out of my door—
35Oh, that I had someone to hear me!
Here is my signature; let the Almighty answer me!
If only I had the charge my accuser has written!
36I would surely carry it on my shoulder;
I would wear it like a crown.
37I would give him an account of every step I have taken;
like a prince I would come near to him.
38If my land has cried out against me,
and its furrows have wept together,
39if I have eaten its yield without payment,
or made its owners breathe their last,
40then let thorns grow instead of wheat,
and foul weeds instead of barley.
The words of Job are ended.
fields.summary: Job swears that he has not lusted, lied, committed adultery, mistreated his servants, neglected the poor or trusted in gold, and asks God to answer him.

fields.title: Job 32
fields.body_html:
Elihu’s anger

1So these three men stopped answering Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes.

2Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the clan of Ram, became angry. He was angry with Job because Job made himself out to be in the right rather than God. 3He was also angry with his three friends, because they had found no answer, and yet they had declared Job guilty. 4Elihu had waited before speaking to Job, because the others were older than he was. 5When Elihu saw that the three men had no answer left, he became angry.

I am young in years

6Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered:
I am young in years, and you are old;
so I held back and was afraid
to tell you what I know.
7I thought, Let age speak,
and let those with many years teach wisdom.
8But it is the spirit in a person,
the breath of the Almighty, that gives understanding.
9It is not the aged who are wise,
nor the old who understand what is right.
10So I say, Listen to me;
let me also tell you what I know.
11Look, I waited while you spoke;
I listened to your arguments
while you searched for what to say.
12I paid close attention to you,
but not one of you refuted Job
or answered his words.
13Do not say, We have found wisdom:
let God refute him, not a human being.
14Job has not directed his words against me,
and I will not answer him with your arguments.
15They are dismayed and answer no more;
they have run out of words.
16Must I wait because they do not speak,
because they stand there and answer no more?
17I too will give my answer;
I too will tell what I know.
18For I am full of words;
the spirit within me drives me on.
19Look, inside I am like wine with no vent;
like new wineskins, I am ready to burst.
20I must speak and find relief;
I must open my lips and answer.
21I will not take anyone’s side,
nor flatter any human being.
22For I do not know how to flatter;
if I did, my Maker would soon carry me away.
fields.summary: Elihu, a young man, angry with Job and with the friends, says that wisdom comes from God’s Spirit and not only from age.

fields.title: Job 33
fields.body_html:
Elihu speaks to Job

1But now, Job, please listen to what I say;
pay attention to all my words.
2Look, I have opened my mouth;
my tongue is forming words in my mouth.
3My words come from an upright heart,
and my lips speak what I know sincerely.
4The Spirit of God has made me;
the breath of the Almighty gives me life.
5Answer me if you can;
prepare your case before me
and take your stand.
6Look, before God I am just as you are;
I too was shaped from clay.
7So no fear of me need terrify you,
and my pressure will not weigh heavily on you.
8You have surely spoken in my hearing,
and I have heard the sound of your words:
9I am pure, without transgression;
I am clean,
and there is no guilt in me.
10Yet God finds reasons to oppose me;
he counts me as his enemy.
11He puts my feet in the stocks;
he watches all my paths.
12But in this you are not right, I tell you,
for God is greater than any human.
13Why do you complain against him
that he answers none of a person’s words?
14For God speaks in one way, and in another,
though people do not notice it.
15In a dream, a vision in the night,
when deep sleep falls on people
as they slumber on their beds,
16then he opens people’s ears
and seals his warning upon them,
17to turn people away from what they are doing
and keep them from pride.
18He spares them from the pit,
their life from perishing by the sword.
19People are also corrected by pain on their beds,
with constant aching in all their bones.
20They come to loathe food,
even the food they most enjoy.
21Their flesh wastes away until it can hardly be seen,
and their bones, once hidden, stick out.
22They draw near to the pit,
their life to those who bring death.
23If there is an angel beside them,
a mediator, one out of a thousand,
to tell them what is right for them,
24and he is gracious to them and says,
Spare them from going down to the pit;
I have found a ransom.
25Their flesh becomes fresher than a child’s;
they return to the days of their youthful strength.
26They pray to God, and he accepts them;
they see his face with shouts of joy,
and he restores them to righteousness.
27Then they sing before others and say,
I sinned and twisted what was right,
but I was not repaid as I deserved.
28God has redeemed them from going down to the pit,
and they will live to see the light.
29Look, God does all these things
two or three times with a person,
30to bring them back from the pit,
so that the light of life may shine on them.
31Pay attention, Job, and listen to me;
be quiet, and I will speak.
32If you have anything to say, answer me;
speak, for I want to see you proved right.
33If not, then listen to me;
be quiet, and I will teach you wisdom.
fields.summary: Elihu says God speaks through dreams and through suffering to turn people from death.

fields.title: Job 34
fields.body_html:
Elihu calls the wise to judge Job’s words

1Then Elihu answered:
2Hear my words, you who are wise;
listen to me, you who have knowledge.
3For the ear tests words
as the tongue tastes food.
4Let us choose for ourselves what is right;
let us decide together what is good.
5For Job has said, “I am in the right,
but God has denied me justice.
6Though I am in the right, I am called a liar;
my wound from the arrow cannot be healed, though I have not rebelled.”
7Who is there like Job,
who drinks up scorn like water?
8He keeps company with evildoers
and goes about with the wicked.
9For he has said, “It does no one any good
to be on good terms with God.”
10So listen to me, you people of understanding:
God would never do evil,
the Almighty would never do wrong.
11For he pays people back for what they do;
he brings on each one what their conduct deserves.
12Truly, God will never do wrong;
the Almighty will never twist justice.
13Who gave him charge over the earth?
Who put him over the whole world?
14If he were to set his mind on himself alone
and gather back to himself his spirit and breath,
15every living thing would die at once,
and human beings would return to dust.
16If you have understanding, hear this;
listen to what I am saying.
17Can one who hates justice rule?
Will you condemn the one who is righteous and mighty?
18Would anyone say to a king, “You worthless man!”
or to nobles, “You wicked men!”?
19How much less to one who shows no favor to princes
and does not regard the rich above the poor,
for they are all the work of his hands!
20In an instant they die; at midnight people are shaken and pass away;
the mighty are removed, and no human hand does it.
21For his eyes are on the ways of everyone;
he sees every step they take.
22There is no darkness, no deep shadow,
where evildoers can hide.
23For he does not need to set a time for anyone
to come before God for judgment.
24He shatters the mighty without any inquiry
and sets others in their place.
25Because he knows what they do,
he overthrows them in the night, and they are crushed.
26He strikes them down for their wickedness
where everyone can see,
27because they turned away from following him
and paid no attention to any of his ways,
28so that they made the cry of the poor reach him,
and he heard the cry of the afflicted.
29If he stays silent, who can condemn him?
If he hides his face, who can see him?
Yet he rules over nation and individual alike,
30so that the godless may not rule
and lay snares for the people.
31Suppose someone says to God, “I have borne my punishment;
I will not do wrong again.
32Teach me what I cannot see;
if I have done wrong, I will do it no more.”
33Should he repay on your terms when you have rejected his way?
You must choose, not I;
so tell us what you know.
34People of understanding will say to me,
and so will any wise person who hears me:
35Job speaks without knowledge;
his words show no insight.
36If only Job were tested to the limit
for answering like the wicked!
37For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands at us in scorn
and piles up his words against God.
fields.summary: Elihu insists that God does no wrong and repays each person by their deeds.

fields.title: Job 35
fields.body_html:
What do you give to God?

1Then Elihu answered:
2Do you think this is right?
You say, “I am more in the right than God.”
3For you ask, “What good is it to me?
What do I gain by not sinning?”
4I will give you an answer,
you and your friends with you.
5Look up at the sky and see;
gaze at the clouds high above you.
6If you sin, what harm do you do him?
If your rebellions are many, what does that do to him?
7If you are righteous, what do you give him?
What does he receive from you?
8Your wickedness affects only people like yourself;
your righteousness, only other human beings.
9People cry out under the weight of oppression;
they call for help against the power of the mighty.
10But no one says, “Where is God my Maker,
who gives songs in the night,
11who teaches us more than the animals of the earth
and makes us wiser than the birds of the sky?”
12There they cry out, but he does not answer,
because of the pride of the wicked.
13Surely God does not listen to an empty cry;
the Almighty pays it no attention.
14How much less will he listen when you say you do not see him,
that your case is before him and you are waiting for him!
15And now, because his anger does not punish,
and he pays little heed to wrongdoing,
16Job opens his mouth with empty talk;
he piles up words without knowledge.
fields.summary: Elihu says human wrongdoing or righteousness does not change God, and that God does not answer empty cries.

fields.title: Job 36
fields.body_html:
Elihu speaks for God once more

1Then Elihu continued:
2Be patient with me a little longer, and I will show you
that there is more to be said on God’s behalf.
3I will draw my knowledge from far and wide,
and I will show that my Maker is in the right.
4Truly, my words are not false;
one whose knowledge is sound is here with you.
5God is mighty, and yet he despises no one;
he is mighty in strength of understanding.
6He does not let the wicked live on,
but he gives the afflicted their rights.
7He does not take his eyes off the righteous;
he seats them with kings on the throne,
and they are raised up forever.
8And if people are bound in chains,
held fast by cords of suffering,
9then he shows them what they have done,
their transgressions, how they have acted with pride.
10He opens their ears to correction
and commands them to turn back from evil.
11If they listen and serve him,
they will spend their days in prosperity
and their years in contentment.
12But if they do not listen, they perish by the sword
and die without understanding.
13But those who are godless at heart hold on to their anger;
they do not cry for help even when he binds them.
14They die in their youth,
and their life ends among the shrine prostitutes.
15He rescues the afflicted through their suffering
and opens their ears through distress.
16He was also drawing you out of the jaws of distress
into a wide place with nothing to hem you in,
to a table loaded with the richest food.
17But now you are full of the judgment due to the wicked;
judgment and justice have taken hold of you.
18Beware that anger does not lure you into scoffing,
and do not let a great ransom turn you aside.
19Can your riches keep you out of distress,
or all your mighty efforts?
20Do not long for the night,
when peoples are taken away from where they are.
21Be careful not to turn to evil,
for you have preferred it to suffering.
22God is exalted in his power;
who is a teacher like him?
23Who has prescribed his path for him,
or who can say to him, “You have done wrong”?
24Remember to praise his work,
which people have celebrated in song.
25Everyone has seen it;
people look on it from far away.
26God is great, beyond our knowing;
the number of his years cannot be searched out.
27For he draws up the drops of water,
which distill as rain from his mist,
28which the clouds pour down
and shower on many people.
29Can anyone understand how the clouds spread out,
or the thunder from his pavilion?
30See how he scatters his lightning around him
and covers the depths of the sea.
31For by these he judges the peoples
and gives food in abundance.
32He fills his hands with lightning
and commands it to strike the mark.
33His thunder announces his coming;
even the cattle sense the storm rising.
fields.summary: Elihu says God uses affliction to teach, and praises God’s greatness shown in the rain and the storm.

fields.title: Job 37
fields.body_html:
God thunders with his voice

1At this my heart pounds
and leaps out of its place.
2Listen, listen to the thunder of his voice,
to the rumbling that comes from his mouth.
3He lets it loose under the whole sky
and sends his lightning to the ends of the earth.
4After it comes a roar;
he thunders with his majestic voice,
and he does not hold back the lightning when his voice is heard.
5God thunders with his voice in wonderful ways;
he does great things beyond our understanding.
6For he says to the snow, “Fall on the earth,”
and likewise to the shower of rain,
the downpour of his mighty rains.
7He brings the work of every person to a stop,
so that all the people he has made may know it.
8The wild animals go into their lairs
and stay in their dens.
9The whirlwind comes out of its chamber,
and cold comes from the driving winds.
10By the breath of God ice is formed,
and the wide waters are frozen fast.
11He loads the thick clouds with moisture;
the clouds scatter his lightning.
12They whirl around at his direction
to carry out all that he commands them
over the face of the whole earth.
13Whether for correction, or for his land,
or for faithful love, he makes it happen.
14Listen to this, Job;
stop and think about God’s wonders.
15Do you know how God gives them their orders
and makes the lightning flash from his cloud?
16Do you know how the clouds hang balanced,
the wonders of the one who is perfect in knowledge?
17You whose clothes grow hot
when the land lies still under the south wind,
18can you join him in spreading out the skies,
hard as a mirror of cast metal?
19Teach us what we should say to him;
we cannot prepare our case, because we are in the dark.
20Should he be told that I want to speak?
Would anyone ask to be swallowed up?
21Now no one can look at the light
when it is brilliant in the skies,
after the wind has passed and swept them clear.
22Out of the north comes golden splendor;
God is clothed in awesome majesty.
23The Almighty is beyond our reach; he is great in power,
and in his justice and great righteousness
he does not oppress.
24That is why people fear him;
he pays no attention to those who think they are wise.
fields.summary: Elihu describes God’s majesty in thunder, snow and lightning, and says the Almighty is beyond our reach.

fields.title: Job 38
fields.body_html:
The LORD answers Job from the storm

1Then the LORD answered Job from the storm:
2Who is this who makes my plan obscure
with words that lack knowledge?
3Brace yourself like a man;
I will question you,
and you will tell me the answers.
4Where were you when I founded the earth?
Tell me, if you have such understanding.
5Who decided how large it would be? You must know!
Or who ran a measuring line across it?
6On what were its footings set down,
or who laid its cornerstone,
7while the morning stars were singing together
and all the sons of God raised a shout of joy?
8Who closed the sea in behind doors
when it burst out
and came forth from the womb,
9when I made the clouds its clothing
and dense darkness the cloth that wrapped it,
10when I marked out my boundary for it
and set in place its bar and doors,
11and said, ‘You may come as far as this and go no further;
here your proud waves will halt’?
12Have you ever in your life given orders to the morning
or shown the dawn its place,
13so that it seizes the earth by its edges
and shakes the wicked out of it?
14The earth takes shape like clay under a seal;
its features stand out like the folds of a garment.
15The wicked are denied their light,
and the arm they raise is broken.
16Have you gone down to the sources of the sea
or walked through the hidden depths of the ocean?
17Have the gates of death been opened to you?
Have you seen the gates of the deepest darkness?
18Have you grasped how wide the earth is?
Tell me, if you know all this.
19Where is the road to the place where light lives?
And darkness, where is its home,
20so that you could lead it to its territory
and know the paths to its home?
21Surely you know, since you were already born then,
and you have lived so many days!
22Have you gone into the storerooms of the snow
or seen the storerooms of the hail,
23which I keep in reserve for times of trouble,
for days of battle and war?
24By what way is the light parceled out,
or the east wind spread across the earth?
25Who carves out a channel for the torrents of rain
and a path for the thunderstorm,
26to bring rain on land where no one lives,
on a wilderness without a human in it,
27to soak the barren, desolate ground
and make the tender grass spring up?
28Does the rain have a father?
Who has fathered the drops of dew?
29From whose womb does the ice come?
And who gives birth to the frost of the sky?
30The waters harden like stone,
and the surface of the deep freezes solid.
31Can you tie together the cluster of the Pleiades
or untie the belt of Orion?
32Can you bring out the constellations at their proper times
or guide the Bear with its cubs?
33Do you know the laws that govern the heavens?
Can you establish their rule over the earth?
34Can you shout an order to the clouds
and have a flood of water cover you?
35Can you send the lightning bolts on their way,
and will they say to you, ‘Here we are’?
36Who has put wisdom in the inner self
or given understanding to the mind?
37Who has the wisdom to count the clouds?
Who can tip over the water jars of the sky
38when the dust has hardened into a solid mass
and the clods cling together?
39Do you hunt down prey for the lioness
or satisfy the hunger of her young lions
40when they crouch in their dens
or lie in wait in the thicket?
41Who supplies the raven with its food
when its young ones cry out to God
and wander about with nothing to eat?
fields.summary: God answers Job out of the storm, asking where he was when the earth was founded, and questions him about the sea, the light, the snow and the stars.

fields.title: Job 39
fields.body_html:
Do you know when the mountain goats give birth?

1Do you know when the mountain goats give birth among the rocks?
Do you watch over the does as they bear their young?
2Can you count the months until they are due,
and do you know the time when they give birth?
3They crouch down and bring their young to birth;
they are rid of their labor pains.
4Their young grow strong and grow up in the open country;
they go off and do not come back to them.
5Who let the wild donkey go free?
Who untied the ropes of the wild ass?
6I made the wilderness its home
and the salt flats its dwelling place.
7It scorns the noise of the city;
it never hears the shouts of a driver.
8It roams the mountains for its pasture
and searches for every green plant.
9Will the wild ox agree to serve you?
Will it stay the night beside your feeding trough?
10Can you tie the wild ox with a rope to plow a furrow?
Will it follow you and break up the soil in the valleys?
11Will you rely on it because its strength is great?
Will you leave your heavy work to it?
12Can you trust it to bring in your grain
and gather it to your threshing floor?
13The ostrich flaps her wings with joy,
but are they the wings and feathers of the stork?
14She leaves her eggs on the ground
and lets them warm in the sand.
15She forgets that a foot may crush them,
that a wild animal may trample them.
16She treats her young harshly, as if they were not hers;
she has no fear that her labor may be wasted.
17For God has made her forget wisdom
and has given her no share of understanding.
18Yet when she rises up to run,
she laughs at the horse and its rider.
19Do you give the horse its strength?
Do you clothe its neck with a flowing mane?
20Do you make it leap like a locust?
Its proud snorting strikes terror.
21It paws the ground in the valley and delights in its strength;
it charges out to meet the weapons.
22It laughs at fear and is not afraid;
it does not turn back from the sword.
23The quiver rattles at its side,
along with the flashing spear and javelin.
24Trembling with excitement, it devours the ground;
it cannot stand still when the horn sounds.
25Whenever the horn blows, it snorts, Aha!
It smells the battle from far away,
the thunder of the commanders and the war cry.
26Is it by your understanding that the hawk takes flight
and spreads its wings toward the south?
27Is it at your command that the eagle flies high
and builds its nest up on the heights?
28It lives on the cliffs and stays there at night,
on a rocky crag, its fortress.
29From there it searches for its prey;
its eyes see it from far away.
30Its young ones gulp down blood,
and where the dead bodies are, there it is.
fields.summary: God asks Job about the wild animals: the mountain goats, the wild donkey, the wild ox, the ostrich, the horse and the hawk.

fields.title: Job 40
fields.body_html:
Job answers the LORD

1Then the LORD answered Job:
2Will the one who finds fault contend with the Almighty?
Let the one who argues against God give an answer.

3Then Job answered the LORD:
4I am so small; how can I answer you?
I put my hand over my mouth.
5I have spoken once, and I will not reply;
twice, and I will say no more.

Will you condemn me so that you may be in the right?

6Then the LORD answered Job from the storm:
7Brace yourself like a man;
I will question you,
and you will tell me the answers.
8Would you really set aside my justice?
Would you condemn me to prove that you are right?
9Do you have an arm like God’s?
Can you thunder with a voice like his?
10Then put on majesty and dignity;
clothe yourself with splendor and glory.
11Unleash the fury of your anger;
look at all who are proud and bring them down.
12Look at all who are proud and humble them;
crush the wicked where they stand.
13Bury them all together in the dust;
shroud their faces in the hidden place.
14Then I myself will admit to you
that your own right hand can save you.
15Look at Behemoth, which I made just as I made you;
it eats grass like an ox.
16See the strength in its hips,
the power in the muscles of its belly!
17Its tail stiffens like a cedar;
the sinews of its thighs are tightly woven.
18Its bones are pipes of bronze,
its limbs like bars of iron.
19It is the first of the works of God;
only its Maker can come near it with his sword.
20The hills bring it their produce,
and all the wild animals play nearby.
21It lies under the lotus plants,
hidden among the reeds of the marsh.
22The lotus bushes cover it with their shade;
the poplars by the stream surround it.
23Even when the river surges, it is not alarmed;
it stays calm though the Jordan rushes against its mouth.
24Can anyone capture it while it is watching,
or pierce its nose with a snare?
fields.summary: Job says he is small and will say no more. God asks whether Job would discredit God’s justice and describes Behemoth.

fields.title: Job 41
fields.body_html:
1Can you pull in Leviathan with a fishhook
or tie down its tongue with a rope?
2Can you put a cord through its nose
or pierce its jaw with a hook?
3Will it keep begging you for mercy?
Will it speak gently to you?
4Will it make a covenant with you
for you to take it as your slave for life?
5Will you play with it as with a pet bird
or put it on a leash for your young girls?
6Will traders bargain over it?
Will they divide it up among the merchants?
7Can you fill its hide with harpoons
or its head with fishing spears?

No one can stand before Leviathan

8Just lay a hand on it,
and you will remember the fight and never do it again.
9Any hope of overpowering it is false;
the mere sight of it lays a person low.
10No one is fierce enough to stir it up;
who then can stand up to me?
11Who has first given to me, that I should pay them back?
Everything under the whole heaven is mine.
12I will not keep silent about its limbs,
its mighty strength and its fine build.
13Who can strip off its outer coat?
Who can come at it with a double bridle?
14Who can pry open the doors of its face?
Its teeth all around are a terror.
15Its pride is its rows of shields,
shut together as with a tight seal.
16Each one is so close to the next
that no air can pass between them.
17They are joined one to another;
they cling together and cannot be pulled apart.
18Its snorting makes light flash out,
and its eyes are like the first rays of dawn.
19Flaming torches pour from its mouth;
sparks of fire shoot out.
20Smoke pours from its nostrils
as from a pot fanned to a boil over burning reeds.
21Its breath sets coals on fire,
and flames dart from its mouth.
22Strength makes its home in its neck,
and terror dances before it.
23The folds of its flesh are tightly joined;
they are set firm on it and do not move.
24Its heart is as hard as rock,
as hard as a lower millstone.
25When it raises itself up, the mighty are afraid;
at its crashing they are thrown into confusion.
26A sword that reaches it has no effect,
nor does a spear, a dart, or a javelin.
27It treats iron like straw
and bronze like rotten wood.
28Arrows do not make it run away;
sling stones are like chaff to it.
29A club seems like chaff to it,
and it laughs at the rattle of a javelin.
30Its underside is like jagged pieces of pottery;
it leaves a trail in the mud like a threshing sledge.
31It makes the depths churn like a boiling pot;
it stirs up the sea like a pot of perfumed oil.
32It leaves a shining wake behind it;
one would think the deep had white hair.
33Nothing on earth is its equal,
a creature made without fear.
34It looks down on everything that is lofty;
it is king over all the proud beasts.
fields.summary: God describes Leviathan, a creature no one can tame.

fields.title: Job 42
fields.body_html:
Job answers the LORD

1Then Job answered the LORD:
2I know that you can do everything;
no purpose of yours can be stopped.
3You asked, “Who is this who hides my plan without knowledge?”
Truly I have spoken of what I did not understand,
things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.
4You said, “Listen now, and I will speak;
I will question you, and you will answer me.”
5I had heard of you by what my ears were told,
but now my own eyes have seen you.
6So I take back what I said,
and I repent in dust and ashes.

The LORD rebukes Job’s friends

7After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My anger burns against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. 8So now take seven bulls and seven rams, go to my servant Job, and offer a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you as your folly deserves. For you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.” 9So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD had told them, and the LORD accepted Job’s prayer. 10When Job prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes, and the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before. 11All his brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before came and ate a meal with him in his house. They showed him sympathy and comforted him for all the trouble the LORD had brought on him, and each of them gave him a piece of money and a gold ring.

The LORD blesses the latter days of Job

12The LORD blessed the last part of Job’s life more than the first. He had 14,000 sheep, 6,000 camels, 1,000 yoke of oxen, and 1,000 female donkeys. 13He also had seven sons and three daughters. 14He named the first Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren-happuch. 15In all the land there were no women as beautiful as Job’s daughters, and their father gave them an inheritance along with their brothers.

16After this Job lived 140 years, and he saw his children and grandchildren to the fourth generation. 17And Job died, old and satisfied with his days.
fields.summary: Job repents in dust and ashes, having heard of God and now seen God. God rebukes the friends, Job prays for them, and God restores Job’s fortunes twice over and blesses his later life.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
After this Job lived 140 years, and he saw his children and grandchildren to the fourth generation. And Job died, old and satisfied with his days.

— Job 42:16–17

Job ends with a long life and a peaceful death, his children’s children around him, and the friends who wronged him forgiven through his prayers. It is a gentle ending to a terrible book, but it is not the answer. The answer came earlier, in the storm, and it was not an explanation. It was God himself.

The question the book leaves with you

The book began with a question asked in heaven: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” By the end, it has been answered. Job lost everything God had given him, and he did not curse God. He complained, wept and demanded a hearing, but he never let go, and when God finally spoke, Job bowed down. The Accuser was wrong. A human being can love God for God’s sake.

But the question does not stay in heaven. It comes down to every reader. Would my faith survive if the hedge came down? Is God, to me, a means to a comfortable life, or is he worth trusting when he gives no reasons? Job does not make that question easy, but it shows that faith is allowed to be honest, that lament is a form of prayer, and that God would rather be argued with than lied about. “You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.”

And Job leaves a second question, one he asked himself. He longed for someone to stand between him and God: an umpire who “could lay his hand on us both”, a witness in heaven, a Redeemer who would stand up for him at the last. Who could that be?

Where the book points

The New Testament gives the answer Job could only reach for:

“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself as a ransom for all.”

— 1 Timothy 2:5–6

Job wanted a go-between who was not “a human being like me” on the one side and yet could understand a human being on the other. In Jesus, God became the mediator Job asked for. More than that, Jesus became the innocent sufferer. He was the one truly blameless man, and he suffered not for his own sins but, as the church has always confessed, for ours. On the cross he cried out to God in the words of a psalm, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”, and Job’s lament became the prayer of the Son of God. The letter to the Hebrews says that we have a high priest who can “share the feeling of our weaknesses”.

Job asked, “If a mortal dies, will they live again?” The empty tomb is God’s reply. Job hoped to see God in his flesh; Christians believe that hope will be fulfilled in the resurrection of the body. And when Paul came to the end of his own long wrestling with God’s ways in Romans 11, he could only break into praise, and he borrowed words from the LORD’s speech to Job to do it: “Or who has given him anything first and must be paid back?”

Where to go from here

Job has been a companion to suffering believers in every age, and some of the best writing on him is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the Redeemer (Job 19). John Newton’s sermon I Know That My Redeemer Liveth (Job 19:25–26).
  • On Job’s complaint and longing (Job 10, 14, 23, 29). Charles H. Spurgeon’s The Sweet Uses of Adversity (Job 10:2), Order and Argument in Prayer (Job 23:3–4) and Comfort for the Desponding (Job 29:2); and George MacDonald’s Unspoken Sermons, whose long sermon “The Voice of Job” begins from Job 14:13–15.
  • On the counsel of the friends and Elihu. Alexander Maclaren’s The Peaceable Fruits of Sorrows Rightly Borne (Job 5:17–27) and What Life May Be Made (Job 22:26–29), and Spurgeon’s Songs in the Night (Job 35:10).
  • On the book as a whole. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Job: The Death of Self” reads the book as the story of a good man brought to the end of himself; and Andrew Murray’s Divine Healing, whose chapter “Job’s Sickness and Healing” begins with Job 2:7.
  • On asking God why. The Key Teachings of Elisabeth Elliot, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “On Asking God Why” turns to Job; and The Key Teachings of Hudson Taylor, whose chapter “Blessed Adversity” follows Taylor’s address on Job.
  • On the hard places of providence. Thomas Boston’s The Crook in the Lot, on bearing what God has sent, which returns again and again to Job; and Boethius’s The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison awaiting execution, long loved by Christian readers as a book on suffering and the good that cannot be taken away.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Job in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And if you are in the ashes yourself, go back to the place where Job, with nothing left and no one on his side, looked up and said the words that believers have been saying at gravesides ever since:

But I know that my Redeemer lives, and that at the last he will stand upon the dust.

— Job 19:25
